rewriteLast.title: Chapter 6 · Grimes’s Tear
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a calm sky-lit cove: a gruff sooty sweep sits hunched on a rock while gentle water-nymphs bathe him with warm silver towels, one big tear rolling down his cheek, a small shiny water-baby watching kindly from the shallows, seabirds wheeling in soft morning haze, silver-and-rose light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: At the Other-End-of-Nowhere, the water grew quiet and grey, and the sky hung low over the rocks. There, all alone, sat Grimes. He was still grim and sooty, and as cross with the whole world as ever. And that made him the loneliest man in it. Tom had come a long, long way to find him.
Grimes weeps one true tear, and Tom forgives him before he even asks.

The gentle water-nymphs came about him like soft silver fish. They bathed Grimes and washed away his grumbles, though he grumbled loudest of anyone, all the while they washed. But under all the grumbling his heart was sore. And at last one big tear rolled down his sooty cheek. It was the first true tear he had ever cried in all his life.

“Why, Master,” said Tom, swimming close, “how do you do?” Grimes stared — and then he knew his little sweep again. It was the boy he had been so unkind to, come all this way to help him. And he wept like rain, and was sorry from the bottom of his heart.
Ask your child: Grimes was unkind to Tom. Why did Tom help him anyway?

“I will be kinder,” said Grimes at last, wiping his eyes with the back of his hand. “Kinder to every little boy I meet, and to every man and beast as well, so long as I live.” Tom believed him. For one true tear, the fairies say, washes a heart cleaner than all the rivers in the world.

Then the fairies lifted Tom softly, and the shining water carried him home. It took him over the bright waves and past the forests of kelp. It took him past the lantern jellyfish. It took him all the way back to the clear river at the foot of the hills. He did not look once behind him. Kind hearts travel light.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Way Home
chapters.artPrompt: a small shiny water-baby and a girl in white swimming side by side through a sunlit sea, past red-and-gold coral gardens and forests of waving green kelp, silver shoals of fish streaming past like ribbons of light, bright morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: On the shore stood a girl in white, tall and kind and glad. It was Ellie, who had watched for Tom all along, and never once given him up. The fairies let the two friends travel home together. The way was long, but good friends make any way seem short.

They swam through seas full of wonders. They passed coral gardens of red and gold, and forests of kelp that waved like tall green grass. Silver shoals of fish went past them like ribbons of light. They went round the great white ice-cliffs where the sea-birds nest. There the wind blew so cold that it nipped their ears, and they laughed and swam faster.
Tom and Ellie swim home together past coral gardens and silver shoals of fish.

At last the water grew warm and golden, and Tom heard a well-known sound. It was the minnows laughing, and the caddis flies rattling their little stone houses. He was home in the clear river, and every neighbour in it came out to meet him. The old caddis fly peeped out of her pebble house, and the minnows swam three times round him for joy.
Ask your child: what is the longest way you have ever travelled? What made the way feel shorter?

Ellie went back to the great Hall on the hill, where the windows shone like amber in the evening sun. But first she stood on the bank above Tom’s pool, and waved. And Tom waved back with his little webbed hand, and splashed her, and the fairies laughed to see them.

From that day the two of them were the very best of friends. And whenever the river ran low and the sun lay hot on the stones, Ellie came down to the pool. She sat with her feet in the water, and told Tom all the news of the world above.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · A Great Man of Science
chapters.artPrompt: a tall kind-faced man in a workshop at night drawing careful plans of bridges and steam-engines and telegraph wires by lamplight, a small glass bowl of river water and a water-lily on his desk, warm golden lamp glow, storybook illustration

blocks.text: So Tom stayed in the river, and grew — not bigger, but wiser and kinder and cleaner of heart. The fairies taught him their water lessons. He learned how the rain is made and how the rivers run. He learned that every little creature has its work to do. Nothing in the pool was too small to be worth his care. And Tom learned them all.

Then, when he was ready, the fairies let Tom go up into the world, to school, and then to work. He studied hard, and asked questions of everything, and never once said “I can’t be bothered.” And when the lessons were hard, he thought of the long swim to the Other-End-of-Nowhere, and did not complain. For a clean heart loves learning, and learning grows happier every day.
Tom, grown tall, draws plans for bridges and steam-engines by lamplight.

When Tom was grown, he became a great man of science. He could plan railways, and steam-engines, and electric telegraphs. And the wires carried words swifter than any horse could run. He could make great things, because he had first learned to do small things well. And he was kind while he did them.
New word: science — learning how the world works, by looking carefully, asking questions and testing what you find.

But Tom never forgot the river. On summer evenings he would leave his plans and pencils. He would walk out to the clear pool where the water-lilies grew. The river was still there, and still clear, and that was the main thing. He would sit quite still on the bank and watch the water shine, just to say thank you to it. And often, people said, he seemed to be watching something that nobody else could see. For he knew better than anyone that the world is full of quiet, kind, wonderful things. You have only to keep your eyes open.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Andromeda
chapters.artPrompt: a grown man and woman standing with a radiant fairy on a high green headland above the sea at night, the fairy pointing up to a bright shape of stars shaped like a maiden above the dark waves, a whole sky of stars, deep blue night light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Ellie grew up too — kind, and clever, and beautiful of heart. She and Tom stayed the best of friends all their days. And on a midsummer evening, when the stars were coming out, the fairy came to walk with them. She led them up a high green headland above the sea.

“Look up,” said the fairy, and pointed with her hand. There in the sky hung a bright shape of stars. It was a maiden, chained to a rock above the dark sea. Behind her a great sea-monster was rising from the waves. “That is Andromeda, the maiden of the oldest story of all,” said the fairy.
On a starry headland, the fairy shows Tom and Ellie the maiden Andromeda shining in the sky above the sea.

“Are there still sea-monsters?” asked Tom. “There is always a sea-monster, dear child,” said the fairy. “But there is always a morning after it, too.” “She was in danger, but she was not afraid,” the fairy went on. “And when the brave prince came, she was set free. So it is, my dears, with everyone who keeps a clean heart: the story ends well at the last.”
New word: constellation — a picture made of stars in the night sky.

Tom and Ellie looked, and the stars seemed to sparkle the brighter. It was as if the maiden were smiling down at them. And when they turned to thank the fairy, she was gone. But the whole sky looked kinder, somehow, than it had before.

And so our story ends. Down below the headland, small and silver, the clear river ran on to the sea. It sang its one little song — clear and cool, clear and cool. It sang to anyone with eyes to see and a heart to hear. And if you keep your heart clean and your eyes open, you may hear it too. Listen beside any water, on a bright morning, and see.
